newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac to honour late U.S. envoy Pamela Harriman.
newsitem.headline: Chirac to honour late U.S. envoy Pamela Harriman.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac will honour the late U.S. ambassador to France Pamela Harriman on Saturday in a quiet ceremony at her Paris residence, an embassy aide said on Thursday.

Harriman, who died on Wednesday of a brain haemorrhage, aged 76, will be presented with France's highest award -- the Grand Cross of the Legion of Honour -- in a ceremony to be attended only by family and embassy personnel, the aide said.

Later on Saturday, her body, accompanied by her son Winston Spencer Churchill, will be flown to Washington for a funeral, probably next week. Churchill, a British MP, had been at her side since she was taken ill.
She is to be buried at Arden House in New York State, former residence of her husband, the late New York governor and U.S. diplomat Averell Harriman.
Last year, France honoured Harriman by making her a Commander of the Order of Arts and Letters for her patronage of fine arts.
Harriman, who had served as Washington's envoy to Paris since 1993, had been planning to retire as ambassador in the next few months.
Speculation on her successor has centred on Frank Wisner, U.S. ambassador to India, and New York investment banker Felix Rohatyn.

An elegant woman who became a respected diplomat after being the wife or companion of some of the world's wealthiest and most powerful men, she was a popular figure in Paris, admired for her fluent French and gracious style.
She had been given the Paris posting by President Bill Clinton after raising millions of dollars for his 1992 election campaign.
Clinton had praised Harriman on Wednesday as "one of the most unusual and gifted people I ever met".

"Our country will miss her," Clinton said. "We are deeply indebted to the work she did in France in maintaining our relationships with one of our oldest and closest allies. She was a source of judgment and inspiration to me, a source of constant good humour and charm and real friendship and we will miss her very very much."
Chirac had taken the unusual step of coming out on the steps of his Elysee Palace on Wednesday to pay her an emotional tribute in English.
"I am very, very sad. She was such a beautiful ambassador, probably one of the best since Ben Franklin and Jefferson, so intelligent, so charming, so elegant," he said.
